[&_blockquote_p::after]:hidden","children":[["$","h3","h3-0",{"children":"Introduction"}],"\n",["$","p","p-0",{"children":["Robert Athlyi Rogers (May 6, 1891 – August 24, 1931), spiritually known as Athlyi, Shepherd of the Athlicans, was an Anguillian-born author, preacher, and religious innovator whose theological writings laid the foundation for modern Black liberation theology. In an era dominated by colonial oppression and racial segregation, Rogers articulated a revolutionary Afrocentric cosmology that challenged the white monopoly on Christian divinity. His landmark text, ",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"The Holy Piby"}]," (1924)—frequently referred to as the \"Black Man's Bible\"—posited that people of African descent were the chosen people of God and prophesied the rise of a Black king in Africa who would lead the global diaspora back to redemption. As the founder of the Afro-Athlican Constructive Church (AACC), Rogers established a religious movement that spread from the industrial cities of New Jersey to the diamond fields of South Africa. Banned by colonial authorities across the Caribbean for its anti-colonial teachings, ",["$","em","em-1",{"children":"The Holy Piby"}]," directly influenced the founders of the Rastafari movement in Jamaica, making Rogers a critical, though often unsung, intellectual father of modern Pan-African spirituality."]}],"\n",["$","h3","h3-1",{"children":"Early Life in Colonial Anguilla"}],"\n",["$","p","p-1",{"children":"Robert Athlyi Rogers was born on May 6, 1891, in the British colony of Anguilla, a small, flat coral island in the northern Caribbean [1]. He was the son of Julia Hodge Rogers and Moses Rogers [2]. During the late nineteenth century, Anguilla was a place of extreme isolation and economic hardship. Administratively joined with St. Kitts and Nevis under a repressive British presidency, Anguilla was largely neglected by the colonial administration."}],"\n","$L9","\n","$La","\n","$Lb","\n","$Lc","\n","$Ld","\n","$Le","\n","$Lf","\n","$L10","\n","$L11","\n","$L12","\n","$L13","\n","$L14","\n","$L15","\n","$L16","\n","$L17","\n","$L18","\n","$L19","\n","$L1a","\n","$L1b","\n","$L1c","\n","$L1d","\n","$L1e","\n","$L1f","\n","$L20","\n","$L21","\n","$L22"]}]]}],"$L23","$L24",false]}],"$L25"]}]
6:["$","script","script-0",{"src":"/_next/static/chunks/2uyb8-0enc77-.js","async":true}]

8:["$","$L26",null,{"children":["$","$27",null,{"name":"Next.MetadataOutlet","children":"$@28"}]}]
9:["$","p","p-2",{"children":"The island’s economy was fragile, relying on subsistence farming, fishing, and salt harvesting from the local salt ponds. The territory was frequently struck by severe droughts and hurricanes, which led to widespread famine and poverty. To survive, many Anguillian men were forced to migrate, traveling throughout the Caribbean and the Americas to find employment."}]
a:["$","p","p-3",{"children":"Growing up in this environment of neglect and resilience, the young Robert developed a deep sense of independence. The spiritual landscape of Anguilla was dominated by the Anglican and Methodist churches, which taught a colonial theology that often reinforced white supremacy and submission to the Crown. Rogers’ early exposure to these structures, combined with the physical and social struggles of his homeland, planted the seeds of a lifelong quest for a theology that validated the humanity and spiritual dignity of Black people."}]
b:["$","h3","h3-2",{"children":"The Wandering Years: Panama and the Pan-African Awakening"}]
c:["$","p","p-4",{"children":"Like many of his contemporaries, Rogers left Anguilla in his youth to seek opportunities abroad [3]. His travels took him through South and Central America, the Caribbean, and eventually to the United States [4]."}]
d:["$","p","p-5",{"children":"A significant portion of his early adulthood was spent in Panama, which was then a hub for West Indian labor during and after the construction of the Panama Canal. In Panama, Rogers was exposed to the brutal labor exploitation and racial segregation imposed by the United States canal administration, where Black workers were paid in the \"silver roll\" system, receiving fractionally lower wages and inferior housing compared to white workers on the \"gold roll.\""}]
e:["$","p","p-6",{"children":"This environment of international Black labor migration was also the breeding ground for early Pan-Africanism. It was in these migration hubs that Rogers encountered the teachings of Marcus Garvey, whose Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA) was mobilizing millions of Black people worldwide. Garvey’s message of racial pride, economic self-reliance, and the redemption of Africa profoundly influenced Rogers. He realized that the political and economic liberation of Black people required a corresponding spiritual liberation—a dismantling of the white colonial image of God."}]
f:["$","h3","h3-3",{"children":"The Composition of \"The Holy Piby\""}]
10:["$","p","p-7",{"children":["Rogers eventually migrated to the United States, settling in the industrial city of Perth Amboy, New Jersey, where a growing community of Afro-Caribbean immigrants resided [3]. It was here that he wrote and published his magnum opus, ",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"The Holy Piby"}],", in 1924 [1]."]}]
11:["$","p","p-8",{"children":[["$","em","em-0",{"children":"The Holy Piby"}]," was presented not merely as a political tract, but as a sacred scripture revealed to Rogers, who took the title of \"Athlyi, Shepherd of the Athlicans.\" The text was a radical reinterpretation of Christian theology, blending biblical stories with Ethiopianism—the belief, rooted in Psalm 68:31 (\"Princes shall come out of Egypt; Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands unto God\"), that Africa was the true spiritual homeland of the Black race."]}]
12:["$","p","p-9",{"children":["$","img","img-0",{"src":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/b8/Anguilla_in_its_region_%28zoom%29.svg","alt":"Zoomed-in locator map of Anguilla, highlighting the territory within the Lesser Antilles where Robert Athlyi Rogers spent his childhood."}]}]
13:["$","p","p-10",{"children":"The book is structured into four distinct sections:"}]
14:["$","ol","ol-0",{"children":["\n",["$","li","li-0",{"children":[["$","em","em-0",{"children":"The First Book of Athlyi Called Athlyi"}],": Outlines the calling of Rogers and the spiritual covenant between God and the \"Ethiopians\" (a term Rogers used to refer to all people of African descent) [5]."]}],"\n",["$","li","li-1",{"children":[["$","em","em-0",{"children":"The Second Book of Athlyi Called Aggregation"}],": Details the theological principles of the movement, proclaiming God as the \"God of the Ethiopians\" and presenting a message of racial unity [5]."]}],"\n",["$","li","li-2",{"children":[["$","em","em-0",{"children":"The Third Book of Athlyi Named The Facts of the Apostles"}],": Elevates political leaders of the Pan-African struggle to the status of divine apostles. Specifically, Rogers identified Marcus Garvey, Robert Lincoln Poston, and Henrietta Vinton Davis (key leaders of the UNIA) as the three apostles of God sent to prepare the way for African redemption [5]."]}],"\n",["$","li","li-3",{"children":[["$","em","em-0",{"children":"The Fourth Book of Athlyi Called Precaution"}],": Offers practical guidance, laws, and prayers for the daily life and governance of the Athlican community [5]."]}],"\n"]}]
15:["$","p","p-11",{"children":["A core prophecy of ",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"The Holy Piby"}]," was the imminent rise of a Black king in Africa who would serve as the redeemer of the race, a prophecy that would play a critical role in the emergence of the Rastafari movement."]}]
16:["$","blockquote","blockquote-0",{"children":["\n",["$","p","p-0",{"children":["\"We, the Ethiopian people, do hereby covenant to stand together in one body for the protection of our race, and to build a nation of our own, that our children may be free from the yoke of the oppressor.\" — ",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"The Holy Piby"}]," [6]"]}],"\n"]}]
17:["$","h3","h3-4",{"children":"The Afro-Athlican Constructive Church and Global Expansion"}]
18:["$","p","p-12",{"children":["To institutionalize the theology of ",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"The Holy Piby"}],", Rogers founded the Afro-Athlican Constructive Church (AACC) in 1925, establishing its headquarters in Perth Amboy, New Jersey [1]. The church was designed to be a self-governing Black institution that promoted spiritual development, cooperative economics, and social welfare."]}]
19:["$","p","p-13",{"children":["Under Rogers' leadership, the AACC established branches in several cities in the United States and the Caribbean. However, the most extraordinary expansion of the church occurred in South Africa. In the mid-1920s, copies of ",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"The Holy Piby"}]," were sent to South Africa, where they found a receptive audience among Black workers in the diamond mining center of Kimberley [7]."]}]
1a:["$","p","p-14",{"children":"A local branch of the AACC was established in Kimberley, known as \"The House of Athlyi,\" located at 253 Nyembane Street [8]. The church's message of a Black God and the spiritual chosenness of Africans resonated deeply with workers facing the oppressive migrant labor system and early segregationist policies of the South African state. The movement grew rapidly, prompting concern from the white South African government, which viewed the Athlican doctrine as a highly dangerous form of anti-colonial subversion and actively worked to suppress the church's activities [9]."}]
1b:["$","h3","h3-5",{"children":"Banning and the Jamaican Connection"}]
1c:["$","p","p-15",{"children":["As the AACC expanded, Rogers’ writings caught the attention of colonial authorities in the West Indies. In Jamaica, the text of ",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"The Holy Piby"}]," was imported by sea captain Charles Goodridge and Grace Jenkins Garrison, who began distributing the book and preaching its doctrines in the late 1920s [7]."]}]
1d:["$","p","p-16",{"children":["The British colonial government in Jamaica, terrified of the potential for labor unrest and anti-colonial rebellion inspired by Garveyism, declared ",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"The Holy Piby"}]," a seditious publication and banned it in 1927. Similar bans were implemented in other British Caribbean colonies. Possessing a copy of the \"Black Man's Bible\" was made a criminal offense, and colonial police actively confiscated and destroyed the books, making original 1924 printings extremely rare."]}]
1e:["$","p","p-17",{"children":["Despite the prohibition, the ideas within ",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"The Holy Piby"}]," spread through underground channels in Jamaica. The book's teachings directly influenced the early pioneers of the Rastafari movement, including Leonard P. Howell, Archibald Dunkley, and Joseph Hibbert. When Ras Tafari Makonnen was crowned as Emperor Haile Selassie I of Ethiopia in 1930, these preachers saw it as the direct fulfillment of Rogers’ prophecy of the rising Black king. Howell’s foundational Rastafarian text, ",["$","em","em-1",{"children":"The Promise Key"}],", drew heavily on the structure, theology, and language of ",["$","em","em-2",{"children":"The Holy Piby"}],", securing Rogers’ place as an architect of Rastafari theology."]}]
1f:["$","h3","h3-6",{"children":"Tragic Demise and Legacy"}]
20:["$","p","p-18",{"children":"The intense pressure of leading a controversial, globally scattered, and politically targeted religious movement took a severe toll on Rogers' mental and physical health. On August 24, 1931, in Perth Amboy, New Jersey, Robert Athlyi Rogers died by suicide at the age of forty [1]. Within the Athlican and Rastafarian traditions, his passing is often spoken of in terms of spiritual transition, describing him as having \"took himself away\" from the trials of the material world."}]
21:["$","p","p-19",{"children":"Following his death, the Afro-Athlican Constructive Church continued to operate, though its influence in the United States waned. However, the theological seeds Rogers planted in the Caribbean and South Africa grew into massive spiritual movements."}]
22:["$","p","p-20",{"children":["Today, Robert Athlyi Rogers is recognized by scholars of religion and African diaspora history as a pioneering theologian who anticipated the Black Theology and Liberation Theology movements of the late twentieth century. His home island of Anguilla, which subsequently fought its own historic revolution in 1967 under leaders like ",["$","$L29","a-0",{"slug":"james-ronald-webster","href":"/profiles/james-ronald-webster","children":"James Ronald Webster"}]," and ",["$","$L29","a-1",{"slug":"atlin-harrigan","href":"/profiles/atlin-harrigan","children":"Atlin Harrigan"}]," to secure its self-determination, remembers Rogers as one of its earliest and most radical global voices. ",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"The Holy Piby"}]," remains a sacred text for millions of Rastafarians worldwide, cementing Rogers' legacy as a shepherd of African spiritual liberation."]}]
23:["$","$L2a",null,{"title":"Learn about the legacy of Robert Rogers","url":"https://caribbeanlegacyarchive.com/profiles/robert-rogers"}]
2b:T45d,Robert Athlyi Rogers was a pioneer of Pan-African theology, Black liberation thought, and Ethiopianist religious philosophy. By compiling and publishing *The Holy Piby* (1924), often called the 'Black Man’s Bible,' Rogers established a revolutionary Afrocentric sacred text that challenged colonial Christian structures, asserted that people of African descent were God's chosen people, and prophesied the rise of a Black redeemer king in Africa. As the founder of the Afro-Athlican Constructive Church (AACC), Rogers established an international religious network that spread self-reliance and racial pride to industrial centers in the United States and the diamond mines of Kimberley, South Africa.

Rogers’ writings had a profound, direct impact on the emergence of the Rastafari movement in Jamaica. Despite being banned by British colonial authorities as seditious, *The Holy Piby* was distributed underground, directly shaping the theology of early Rastafari founders like Leonard P. Howell, who used Rogers’ text as a foundation for Rastafarian scripture and the divinization of Emperor Haile Selassie I.24:["$","div",null,{"className":"mb-12 pt-12 border-t border-gold/10","children":[["$","h2",null,{"className":"font-serif font-bold text-3xl text-navy mb-6","children":"Major Contributions"}],["$","div",null,{"className":"text-navy/80 text-xl leading-relaxed bg-white p-8 border-l-4 border-tropical-green shadow-sm","children":"$2b"}]]}]
